newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK firms gets cheaper funds.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK firms gets cheaper funds.

text.p: Hong Kong's Cheung Kong on Friday became the latest of the territory's blue chip borrowers to get funding at a fine price.
Cheung Kong Finance Co mandated four banks to arrange a HK$3.6 billion term loan facility guaranteed by Cheung Kong Holdings.
The arrangers are BA Asia, CEF Capital, Hang Seng Finance and Societe Generale Asia.

The five-year amortising loan will be repaid by five equal semi-annual installments after a three-year grace period. It pays a margin of 45 basis points per annum over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate.
Bankers said the loan has an average life of four years and pays an all-in return of 56 basis points.
That's about 20 basis points tighter than a similar HK$3.96 billion loan for Cheung Kong launched in March 1996.
Last week, Kerry Holdings announced a US$500 million loan and revolving credit.

The US$400 million five-year loan portion pays a margin of 70 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate for lenders of U.S. dollars and 75 basis points over HIBOR for lenders of Hong Kong dollars.

With fees, bankers said the all-in return is in the mid to high 80s. Sources said it is difficult to directly compare Kerry's latest deal to its prior transactions because the company has undergone a restructuring, but they said the pricing on the new deal is much less generous.

Despite the much tighter pricing, bankers said they expected the deals to go well. But other issuers may have a harder time later this year if banks find that the return on loans offers too small a spread over their own cost of funds.
"The market appetite certainly is good and pricing will continue to come down," predicted one banker.
"But the final test will come when the banks finally say no," she said.
Bankers said Hong Kong property developer Hysan Development Co set the stage this year with its planned HK$2.0 billion five-year floating rate note issue.
The FRN reportedly pays a coupon of 56.5 basis points over HIBOR and an all-in of 64 basis points.
With Hysan paying just 64 basis point, many bankers said they shuddered to think what top-notch borrowers such as Sun Hung Kai might expect when it next comes to market.
Sun Hung Kai paid 75 basis points all-in for a five-year loan last May.
Bankers said CITIC Pacific is quietly seeking a US$1 billion bridge facility to help fund its purchase of China Light and Power shares. They said the loan is likely to be completed as a club deal.
The loan is seen having a tenor of six months to one year.
While no formal mandate has been announced, bankers said five banks -- Hongkong Bank, Hang Seng Bank, Chase Asia, J.P. Morgan and BNP -- are tipped to arrange a deal for CITIC.
The five banks either declined comment or could not be reached. CITIC Pacific also was unavailable for comment.
In other news, Sri Lanka reportedly has mandated its US$50 million floating rate note issue to Citicorp and ING Barings. The deal would be Sri Lanka's first capital markets issue is many years.
Bankers said South Korea's Daehan Bank has mandated a US$100 million floating rate certificate of deposit but terms won't be set until the Hanbo troubles are sorted out.
Land Bank of the Philippines' US$200 million FRN mandate reportedly went to ING Barings.
